title: Frelick, Pratt Power Brewers Past Rays 5-4, Seizing 2-0 World Series Lead
body:
Milwaukee rallied from a four‑run hole in the seventh inning to beat Tampa Bay 5‑4 on Tuesday, giving the Brewers a 2‑0 edge in the World Series. Sal Frelick’s first homer in three months knotted the game at 4‑4, and Cooper Pratt’s clutch single a few batters later supplied the decisive run. The comeback marked the second time this series has seen Milwaukee erase a four‑run deficit, underscoring a resilience that could define the championship.

The game began with Tampa Bay’s offense firing on all cylinders. After a leadoff double, the Rays loaded the bases and capitalized on a single to take a 3‑0 lead in the first inning. A two‑run double in the third stretched the advantage to 5‑0, and the Brewers appeared to be on the back foot. Milwaukee’s starter, Aaron Ashby, struggled to find his rhythm, yielding five hits and three walks before being pulled after six innings. Meanwhile, Tampa Bay’s bullpen kept the pressure on, limiting the Brewers to a single run in the first three innings.

Milwaukee’s response was anchored by a series of timely adjustments. In the fourth inning, the Brewers finally got on the board when William Contreras singled and advanced on a sacrifice bunt, eventually scoring on a ground‑out. The spark ignited a rally that saw the lineup adopt a more aggressive approach, taking extra bases and applying pressure on the Ray’s defense. By the sixth, the Brewers had trimmed the deficit to 5‑2, with a two‑run double by Brice Harvey that highlighted the team’s depth and willingness to capitalize on any mistake.

The turning point arrived in the top of the seventh. With two outs and runners on first and second, Frelick, who had been a defensive stalwart all series, stepped up to the plate. He launched a fastball over the left‑field wall, his first home run since late June, knotting the score at 5‑5. The homer not only erased the four‑run gap but also shifted momentum dramatically. Tampa Bay’s pitcher, Ryan Yarbrough, appeared rattled, and the Rays’ offense stalled as Milwaukee’s defense tightened, turning double plays and making routine outs with precision.

After the tie, the Brewers seized the initiative. A patient at‑bat by Cooper Pratt resulted in a single to left field that drove in the go‑ahead run. Pratt, who has been a quiet but reliable presence in the lineup, displayed the poise of a veteran, sprinting home on a wild pitch that followed his hit. The Rays managed to load the bases in the bottom of the seventh, but a double play followed by a strikeout extinguished any chance of a comeback. In the eighth and ninth, Milwaukee’s relievers, notably Trevor Kelley and Josh Hader, shut the door, allowing just one hit and preserving the 5‑4 lead.

The victory not only gives the Brewers a two‑game cushion but also sends a psychological message to Tampa Bay. Overcoming a four‑run deficit twice in a series is rare; the last team to achieve that feat in a World Series was the 1996 Yankees. Milwaukee’s manager, Pat Maldonado, praised his squad’s “never‑say‑die” attitude, emphasizing that the team’s confidence stems from a combination of seasoned veterans and emerging talent. The win also highlights the strategic flexibility of the Brewers’ coaching staff, who made decisive bullpen moves and encouraged aggressive baserunning that paid dividends.

Looking ahead, the series shifts back to Tampa Bay for Game 3, where the Rays will aim to rebound from the collapse. Their offense, which has been prolific all season, will need to regain composure and capitalize on early scoring opportunities. Meanwhile, Milwaukee will look to maintain its momentum, trusting its bullpen depth and the clutch performances of players like Frelick and Pratt. If the Brewers can continue to weather early deficits and execute under pressure, they stand poised to extend their lead and potentially clinch the championship before the series returns to Milwaukee.
